diagrams.label: Diagrams
diagrams.intro: Every project report needs diagrams. Learn what each diagram shows, when to use it and how to draw it step by step. All examples use the same sample project, FindIt (a campus lost and found app), so you can see how the diagrams fit together.

lessons.title: Which diagram do I need?
lessons.lead: Each diagram answers one question about your system. Pick the ones your marking scheme asks for, then draw them in this order.

head: Diagram
Question it answers
Where it goes in the report
rows: Who uses the system and what can they do?
What data goes in and out of the system?
What are the steps of one process?
What data do we store and how is it related?
Exactly which tables, columns and keys?
Which classes exist in the code and how do they relate?
In what order do the parts talk for one action?
What are the big parts and how do they connect?

items.title: Start from the requirements
items.text: Draw the use case diagram first. Every other diagram must support these use cases.

items.title: Model the data
items.text: ER diagram, then turn it into the database schema.

items.title: Design the system
items.text: Architecture, then class and sequence diagrams for the most important features.

items.title: Check consistency
items.text: Names must match across diagrams: an entity called ITEM should not become Product somewhere else.

items.title: draw.io (diagrams.net)
items.text: Free, works in the browser and saves to Google Drive or GitHub. Has UML, ER and network shapes.

items.title: Lucidchart
items.text: Easy drag and drop with a free education plan. Great for team editing.

items.title: dbdiagram.io
items.text: Type your tables as text and it draws the schema for you. Can export SQL.

items.title: PlantUML / Mermaid
items.text: Write diagrams as code and keep them in Git next to your project.

blocks.text: Every diagram in your report needs a number, a caption and a sentence in the text that explains it: "Figure 4.2 shows the use case diagram".

lessons.title: ER diagrams (entity relationship)
lessons.lead: An ER diagram shows the things your system stores (entities), their details (attributes) and how they are connected (relationships).

blocks.caption: Figure: ER diagram for FindIt in Chen notation

items.title: Entity
items.text: A thing you store many of: STUDENT, ITEM, CLAIM. Drawn as a rectangle. Use a singular noun.

items.title: Attribute
items.text: A detail of an entity: name, email, status. Drawn as an ellipse. The key attribute is underlined.

items.title: Relationship
items.text: How two entities are connected: a student reports items. Drawn as a diamond with a verb.

items.title: Cardinality
items.text: How many: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. One student reports many (N) items.

items.title: List the nouns
items.text: Read your requirements and underline nouns. Keep the ones you must store data about.

items.title: Add attributes
items.text: For each entity, list what you need to know. Pick a unique key (e.g. student_id).

items.title: Connect them
items.text: Ask "how is A related to B?" and write a verb in a diamond.

items.title: Add cardinality
items.text: Ask both directions: one student reports how many items? One item is reported by how many students?

items.title: Resolve M:N
items.text: A many-to-many relationship becomes its own entity in the database (e.g. CLAIM between STUDENT and ITEM).

do: Use singular names in capitals for entities
Underline the key attribute
Label every relationship with a verb
Show cardinality on every line
dont: Draw tables with data types (that is the schema)
Use the same name for two different things
Cross lines when you can move a shape

blocks.text: Crow's foot notation (used by Lucidchart and dbdiagram.io) shows the same information with lines instead of diamonds. Ask your supervisor which notation they prefer and use only one.

lessons.title: EER diagrams (enhanced ER)
lessons.lead: EER adds inheritance to an ER diagram: when several entities share common details, put them in a superclass and show the subclasses.

blocks.caption: Figure: USER is specialised into STUDENT, STAFF and ADMIN

head: Idea
Meaning
How it is drawn
rows: The general entity with shared attributes (USER)
Normal entity rectangle at the top
A special kind of the superclass with extra attributes (STUDENT)
Rectangle below, linked through a circle
A user can be only one subclass
A user can be several subclasses at once
Every superclass row must belong to a subclass
Some rows belong to no subclass

items.title: Find shared attributes
items.text: If STUDENT and ADMIN both have name, email and password, they share a superclass.

items.title: Draw the superclass
items.text: Put the shared attributes and the key on USER.

items.title: Add the subclasses
items.text: Only the extra attributes go on each subclass (student_no, access_level).

items.title: Decide the constraints
items.text: Disjoint or overlapping? Total or partial? Write the reason in your report.

blocks.text: Specialisation is top-down (split USER into types). Generalisation is bottom-up (notice STUDENT and STAFF are similar and create USER). The diagram looks the same.

lessons.title: System architecture diagrams
lessons.lead: The architecture diagram is the map of your whole system: the apps, the server, the database, outside services and how they talk.

blocks.text: Use the **C4 model** to keep it simple: **Context** (your system as one box with its users and outside systems), **Containers** (each app, server and database), **Components** (the main parts inside one container) and **Code**. Most student reports need the first two levels.

items.title: Draw the users
items.text: Who uses the system? Students, admins, staff.

items.title: Add each container
items.text: Mobile app, website, API server, database. Write the technology in each box.

items.title: Add outside services
items.text: Email, payment, maps, AI APIs, cloud storage.

items.title: Connect and label
items.text: Every arrow says what travels on it: HTTPS/JSON, SQL, SMTP.

items.title: Add a legend
items.text: Explain colours and shapes so anyone can read it.

do: Name the technology in each box
Label every arrow
Keep it on one page
Show where the data is stored
dont: Draw every class (that is the class diagram)
Mix two levels of detail in one diagram

lessons.title: Database schema diagrams
lessons.lead: The schema is the exact design of your database: every table, column, data type and key. It comes from your ER diagram.

blocks.caption: Figure: FindIt database schema with primary and foreign keys

items.title: One table per entity
items.text: STUDENT becomes users, ITEM becomes items.

items.title: Columns and types
items.text: Each attribute becomes a column with a type: varchar, int, date, uuid, boolean.

items.title: Primary keys
items.text: Every table gets a unique id (PK).

items.title: Foreign keys
items.text: The "many" side stores the id of the "one" side: items.reporter_id → users.id.

items.title: Normalise
items.text: Remove repeated data. Each fact should be stored in one place only (aim for 3NF).

blocks.title: The same tables written for dbdiagram.io

items: Every table has a primary key
Every relationship has a foreign key on the many side
Column names are consistent (snake_case or camelCase, not both)
No column stores a list of values
Data types are realistic (dates are date, not text)

lessons.title: Use case diagrams
lessons.lead: A use case diagram shows who uses the system (actors) and what they can do (use cases). It is usually the first diagram in your requirements.

items.title: Actor
items.text: A person or outside system that uses yours. Stick figure outside the system box.

items.title: Use case
items.text: A goal the actor achieves, written as verb + noun: "Report lost item". Oval inside the box.

items.title: «include»
items.text: A step that always happens as part of another use case (Approve claim always sends a notification).

items.title: «extend»
items.text: An optional extra (Upload photo sometimes happens while reporting an item).

items.title: Draw the system boundary
items.text: A rectangle with your system name.

items.title: Find the actors
items.text: Who logs in? Which outside systems are involved?

items.title: List each actor's goals
items.text: One oval per goal, verb first.

items.title: Connect actors to their use cases
items.text: Plain lines, no arrows.

items.title: Add include/extend only where it helps
items.text: Keep the diagram readable.

do: Start every use case with a verb
Keep actors outside the box
Match each use case to a functional requirement
dont: Draw the order of steps (that is an activity diagram)
Add 30 use cases to one diagram

lessons.title: UML class diagrams
lessons.lead: A class diagram shows the classes in your code, their attributes and methods, and how they relate: inheritance, association and multiplicity.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Public method with parameters and return type
Composition: the part cannot exist without the whole
Aggregation: the part can exist on its own

items.title: Start from your ER diagram
items.text: Entities usually become classes.

items.title: Add behaviour
items.text: What can each class do? Those are the methods.

items.title: Show inheritance
items.text: Shared attributes move up to a parent class.

lessons.title: UML sequence diagrams
lessons.lead: A sequence diagram shows the order of messages between parts of the system for one action, from top (first) to bottom (last).

items.title: Pick one use case
items.text: For example "Claim an item". One diagram per important use case.

items.title: Put the participants on top
items.text: The actor, then app, API and database from left to right.

items.title: Draw messages in order
items.text: Solid arrows for calls, dashed arrows for replies. Number them.

items.title: Add alt and loop boxes
items.text: Use an alt frame for if/else (e.g. item already claimed) and loop for repeats.

blocks.text: Use real names from your code (POST /claims, ClaimService.create) so the examiner can see the design matches the implementation.

lessons.title: Activity diagrams
lessons.lead: An activity diagram is a flowchart for one process: start, actions, decisions and end. Swimlanes show who does each step.

items.title: Start and end
items.text: Filled circle to start, ringed circle to finish.

items.title: Action
items.text: Rounded rectangle with a verb: "Save item".

items.title: Decision
items.text: Diamond with guards on each path: [valid] / [invalid].

items.title: Fork and join
items.text: A thick bar where steps happen at the same time.

lessons.title: Data flow diagrams (DFD)
lessons.lead: A DFD shows how data moves through the system. Level 0 (the context diagram) shows the whole system as one process; level 1 breaks it into the main processes.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: External entity (a person or system outside yours)
Data store (a table or file), used from level 1
Data flow, always labelled with the data it carries

do: Label every arrow with data ("claim details"), not actions
Number the processes
Keep level 0 to one process
dont: Show decisions or order (DFDs are not flowcharts)

docs.title: Writing test cases and a test report
docs.lead: A test report proves your system works. It lists your test cases, what happened, the bugs you found and whether the system is ready.

blocks.text: A **test case** checks one behaviour: given a starting state and an input, what should happen? A **test report** summarises all the test cases after you run them.

head: Field
What to write
Example
rows: 1. Tap Report  2. Fill the form  3. Tap Save

items.title: Write test cases from the requirements
items.text: At least one per functional requirement, plus wrong-input cases.

items.title: Include negative tests
items.text: Wrong password, empty form, huge file, no internet.

items.title: Run them and record honestly
items.text: Fill in the actual result and status. Add screenshots for failures.

items.title: Log the bugs
items.text: Give each bug an ID, severity and status (open or fixed).

items.title: Summarise
items.text: Totals, pass rate, the most important bugs and your recommendation.

do: Link every test case to a requirement
Write steps someone else can repeat
Report failures and how you fixed them
dont: Write "it works" as the expected result

blocks.text: Use the Test cases sheet to write and run your cases, then the Test report template to present the results in your final report.

docs.title: Writing an interim progress report
docs.lead: Halfway through the project, an interim report shows your supervisor what is done, what is left, what changed and how you will finish on time.

items.title: Remind the reader
items.text: Project title, problem and objectives in a few lines.

items.title: Work completed
items.text: What is finished, with evidence (screenshots, links, test results).

items.title: Work in progress and remaining
items.text: Compare with your roadmap milestones.

items.title: Changes and problems
items.text: What changed from the proposal and why. Each problem with its solution.

items.title: Updated timeline and risks
items.text: New dates for late milestones and how you will catch up.

blocks.text: Your ProjectMentor roadmap already has your milestones and progress. Use it as the evidence for the timeline section.

docs.title: Writing a software design document
docs.lead: The design document explains HOW you will build the system: architecture, data, interfaces and the reasons behind each decision.

head: Section
What goes in it
rows: Purpose, scope and the requirements it is based on
Architecture diagram and the main technology choices with reasons
Class and sequence diagrams for the main features
Wireframes or screenshots of the main screens, API endpoints
How you handle login, passwords, validation and errors

blocks.text: For every big decision, write one sentence on why you chose it and what you rejected. Examiners mark the reasons, not just the choice.

docs.title: Writing a user manual
docs.lead: A user manual helps a real person use your system without you. Write it for someone who has never seen it.

items.title: Know the reader
items.text: Students, admins and staff need different sections.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: How to install or open it, create an account and log in.

items.title: One task per section
items.text: "How to report a lost item" with numbered steps and a screenshot for each step.

items.title: Troubleshooting and FAQ
items.text: Common problems and what to do.

do: Use numbered steps
Show a screenshot for each important step
Use the exact button names
dont: Assume the reader knows the system

templates.name: Test report
templates.when: After you run your test cases, before the final report.

templates.name: Interim progress report
templates.when: Halfway through the project, or when your supervisor asks for progress.
